data.title: <![CDATA[Building an Organization that can Absorb the Pace of Change]]>
<![CDATA[The US Drug-Pricing Reset: Competing on Net Value ]]>
data.description:
US drug pricing has crossed an important threshold. The issue is no longer whether intervention occurs, the question is how several interventions interact with portfolio strategy, evidence generation, contracting, and supply continuity.

These interventions include Medicare negotiation, inflation rebates, benefit redesign, pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) oversight, direct-to-consumer cash channels, and international-reference initiatives.

The durable industry response is not simply lower list prices. It is competition on auditable net value: clinically differentiated products, transparent channel economics, patient-centered benefit design, and reliable supply.

Affordability pressure remains structural

The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) reports that retail prescription-drug spending reached $467.0 billion in 2024, 7.9% above 2023, and projects $518.7 billion for 2025, an 11.1% increase. The forecast reflects utilization and mix, including diabetes and obesity medicines, not price inflation alone.

It also excludes medicines administered in hospitals and physician offices, so it understates the full pharmaceutical market.1,2 IQVIA’s broader all-channel series places 2025 net medicine spending at $606 billion and attributes $14 billion of that year’s growth to glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide/glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) agonists.3

Patient experience remains disconnected from aggregate net-price moderation. In a 2026 KFF poll, 43% of adults reported at least one cost-saving behavior involving medicines; 27% did not fill a prescription and 19% cut pills or skipped doses.

The burden was higher among uninsured and lower-income adults and among Black respondents.4 RAND’s mix-adjusted comparison helps locate the problem: in 2022, US manufacturer gross prices were 2.78 times those in 33 comparison countries overall and 4.22 times as high for originator brands, while unbranded generics were cheaper in the United States.5

The strategic implication is that “price” must always be qualified. Wholesale acquisition cost (WAC), payer net cost, manufacturer net revenue, cash price, patient out-of-pocket cost, and total episode cost are different measures.

A policy or contract can improve one while worsening another. Leaders should demand stakeholder-specific evidence rather than rely on a single discount percentage.

Medicare negotiation is now an operating reality

The first 10 Medicare maximum fair prices (MFPs) took effect on January 1, 2026. CMS estimates that applying them to 2023 utilization would have reduced Medicare net covered-drug spending by $6.0 billion, or 22%, and projects $1.5 billion in 2026 beneficiary out-of-pocket savings.

These figures are a historical counterfactual and a projection — not measured 2026 savings. The MFP discounts of 38%–79% against 2023 WAC are real price benchmarks, but they do not represent reductions from confidential pre-MFP net prices.6

The program is expanding. Fifteen agreed MFPs take effect in 2027; CMS estimates they would have reduced 2024 net spending by $12.0 billion, or 44%, excluding Coverage Gap Discount Program spending. The 2028 cycle, the first to include Part B drugs, covers 15 selected products plus Tradjenta (linagliptin) for renegotiation. CMS had not published prices by September 7, 2026.7,8

Part D redesign changes the market beyond negotiated products. The annual beneficiary out-of-pocket threshold is $2,100 in 2026, and the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan permits interest-free monthly smoothing without reducing total liability.9

Inflation rebates are also operational. CMS assessed more than $1.2 billion owed for the first two Part D periods and $136 million across the first two Part B calendar years. These assessed amounts are neither confirmed collections nor point-of-sale savings.10,11

For manufacturers, MFP exposure now belongs in indication sequencing, evidence plans, channel forecasts, and lifecycle investment reviews. For plans and providers, formulary compliance, pharmacy reimbursement, patient communication, and medical-versus-pharmacy-benefit migration require equal attention.

The relevant metric is not the announced discount alone, but access, adherence, net budget impact, and outcomes after implementation.

PBM reform is shifting from transparency rhetoric to auditability

Concentration makes channel economics central. Federal Trade Commission (FTC) staff reported that the three largest PBMs processed nearly 80% of ~6.6 billion US prescriptions in 2023.

Their affiliated pharmacies received 68% of specialty-drug dispensing revenue, up from 54% in 2016. In a selected sample of 51 specialty generics, FTC staff estimated more than $7.3 billion in affiliated-pharmacy dispensing revenue above the National Average Drug Acquisition Cost from 2017 to 2022.

That figure is neither audited profit nor a sector-wide estimate, but it illustrates how value can move within a vertically integrated organization.12 Rebates are similarly distributional.

The US Government Accountability Office found $48.6 billion in Part D manufacturer rebates in 2021. For 79 of the 100 most-rebated drugs, beneficiaries paid more than plan sponsors after rebates because patient liability was generally calculated from the prerebate price.13

Yet rebates can also restrain premiums. Eliminating one payment stream without controlling replacement administrative fees may redistribute cost rather than reduce it.

The 2026 federal appropriations law therefore matters less as a slogan than as an information architecture. Its key group-plan contract conditions, generally effective August 3, 2028, require detailed reporting, audit rights, and 100% remittance of rebates and related remuneration in covered arrangements and allow transparent bona fide service fees.14

Winning models reconcile every dollar across manufacturer, PBM, plan, pharmacy, and patient. Transparency that cannot be audited at claim and contract level is marketing, not reform.

Cash-pay and international-reference initiatives remain partial

Since 2025, the federal executive agenda has added most-favored-nation targets, manufacturer agreements, and direct-to-consumer access to the pricing toolkit. By August 2026, the administration reported agreements with 26 manufacturers covering 89% of the branded market.15

data.title: <![CDATA[Hims & Hers Partners with Eli Lilly to Sell Obesity Medicines ]]>
data.description:
Eli Lilly and Company and Hims & Hers Health, Inc. hentered an agreement to help expand access to Zepbound (tirzepatide) and Foundayo (orforglipron).

Under the agreement, eligible patients who receive a prescription from a licensed provider on the Hims & Hers platform will be able to access the same self-pay prices available to any patient, without leaving the platform.1 Previously patients were forced to leave the site and were directed to , the company’s direct to consumer platform, if they wanted to purchase the medicines.2

How does the arrangement work?

The agreement combines Eli Lilly’s obesity medicines with Hims & Hers’ consumer platform, allowing patients to complete a consultation, receive a prescription if their provider determines it’s appropriate, and have the FDA-approved medicine shipped directly to their home in a single experience.1 Self-pay pricing starts at $149 per month for Foundayo and $299 per month for Zepbound.

data.title: <![CDATA[Novo Terminates Research Collaboration With Korro Bio ]]>
data.description:
In a filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, Korro Bio, Inc. disclosed it has received written notice from Novo, of the company’s election to terminate the research collaboration and license agreement between the two companies.

According to the filing, Novo is electing to terminate the collaboration for convenience and under the agreement’s terms, Novo is entitled to terminate without cause upon 90 days’ prior written notice.1 The termination is set to become effective on February 1, 2027.

What did the collaboration cover?

Under the original agreement, Korro granted Novo an exclusive worldwide license to research, develop, manufacture, and commercialize certain licensed compounds and products tied to an initial target in the cardiometabolic field, along with a second target Novo had the right to nominate within a specified window.2 Novo never nominated a second target.

As part of the deal, Korro received a $10 million upfront payment and reimbursement of certain research and development costs, along with receiving eligibility for development and commercial milestone payments plus tiered royalties on net sales.1,2 No milestone payments were earned under the agreement at any point.

data.title: <![CDATA[FDA Grants Accelerated Approval to Rybrevant Faspro in Head and Neck Cancer]]>
data.description:
The FDA granted accelerated approval on Nov. 5 to Johnson & Johnson’s Rybrevant Faspro (amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj) for adults with recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma whose disease has progressed on or after platinum-based chemotherapy and an immune checkpoint inhibitor.1 The single-agent indication gives clinicians a subcutaneous option in a setting with few therapies.

The product is a bispecific antibody directed at epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) and mesenchymal-epithelial transition (MET) pathways, and this is its first indication outside lung cancer.1 The label excludes patients with human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma, and continued approval may depend on a confirmatory trial.1

“Outcomes remain poor for patients whose head and neck cancer progresses, and treatment options are limited,” said Barbara Burtness, M.D., medical oncologist and professor of medicine at Yale Cancer Center in New Haven, Connecticut.1

What did the OrigAMI-4 trial show in previously treated patients?

The approval rests on cohort 1 of OrigAMI-4, an open-label, multicenter phase 1b/2 study that gave single-agent amivantamab and hyaluronidase-lpuj to 102 patients who had received platinum-based chemotherapy and an immune checkpoint inhibitor. Patients with HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancer were excluded.

Participants received weight-based doses every three weeks until progression or unacceptable toxicity.1 The primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR) and the secondary endpoint was duration of response, both assessed by blinded independent central review.1

Confirmed ORR was 42% (95% confidence interval, 32% to 52%), including complete responses in 15% of patients and partial responses in 28%.1 Among responders, 56% maintained a response for more than six months.1

Investigators reported the results in the Journal of Clinical Oncology.2

What safety findings accompany the approval?

The most common adverse reactions, occurring in at least 20% of patients, were rash (79%), fatigue (39%), nail toxicity (35%), stomatitis (32%) and edema (28%).1 Serious adverse reactions occurred in 39% of patients, and 6% had fatal adverse reactions, including sudden death in 2% and single cases of myocardial ischemia, tumor hemorrhage, aspiration pneumonia and interstitial lung disease.1

data.title: <![CDATA[ANI Pharmaceuticals to Acquire Egetis Therapeutics, Egetis Sells Priority Review Voucher for $190 Million]]>
data.description:
ANI Pharmaceuticals, Inc. has sent a recommended public offer to acquire Egetis Therapeutics AB (publ), a commercial-stage pharmaceutical company focused on rare diseases.

The offer includes $1.13 per share in cash for Egetis shares, plus cash consideration for outstanding convertible debt and warrants, representing a 27% premium to the 60-day volume-weighted average price.1 The value of the offer, including outstanding incentive programs, amounts to approximately $560 million, and is adjusted for estimated net proceeds from Egetis’s separate priority review voucher sale, with the deal reflecting an enterprise value of approximately $434 million.1,3

Egetis’s lead product, Emcitate, was approved by the European Commission on February 12, 2025, and by FDA on September 28, 2026, as the first and only approved treatment for peripheral thyrotoxicosis in adults and pediatric patients with MCT8 deficiency (Allan–Herndon–Dudley syndrome). ANI is estimating the peak sales potential for Emcitate to reach more than $300 million in its approved indication, with durable protection into 2045 supported by new chemical entity exclusivity, orphan drug exclusivity in both the U.S. and Europe, and an Orange Book-listed patent.1
